intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene (138322) on chromosome 19p13.3.

checks.claim: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The first (c.587+5G>A) was inherited from the mother, and the second (c.588-8_588-4del) was de novo (NM_001039848.1); both were predicted to impact splicing of GPX4.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports GPX4 as the cause and describes two different variants in one child, which is consistent with compound heterozygosity, although it does not establish their phase. In the second family both parents carry the same stop mutation, which would make that child homozygous, not compound heterozygous. 'Compound heterozygous' is therefore not the abstract's term and does not fit both families.

checks.claim: The GPX4 gene is located on chromosome 19p13.3.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the enzyme glutathione peroxidase 4 cause Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard gene nomenclature added by the draft and is acceptable.

paragraphs.text: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type is a rare congenital skeletal dysplasia (Aygun et al., 2012) that is lethal in the neonatal period (Smith et al., 2014). Opitz et al. (1987) suggested autosomal recessive inheritance. Radiologic findings include metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (Koutouby et al., 2000), mild rhizomelic shortness of the limbs, platyspondyly, and 'laciness' of the iliac wings (Peeden et al., 1992). Affected infants may have cardiorespiratory insufficiency (Sedaghatian, 1980) and cardiac conduction defects (Smith et al., 2014). Aygun et al. (2012) suggested that central nervous system malformations might be a major component of the disorder, and English et al. (2006) raised the possibility of neuronal migration abnormalities. Koutouby et al. (2000) noted that all previously reported cases had died within 4 days of life, although their patient survived 161 days.

paragraphs.text: English et al. (2006) reported an infant who experienced recurrent cyanotic episodes within a few hours of delivery. The authors suggested a novel association of the disorder with agenesis of the corpus callosum and highlighted the possibility of neuronal migration abnormalities in the disorder.

paragraphs.text: Opitz et al. (1987) noted the occurrence of the disorder in children of both sexes born to normal parents who were first cousins, and suggested that Sedaghatian syndrome is an autosomal recessive trait. Peeden et al. (1992) noted that the infant reported by Opitz et al. (1987) was born to first cousins, suggesting an autosomal recessive single gene defect. Smith et al. (2014) identified biallelic truncating GPX4 mutations in an affected child.

checks.evidence_quote: In vitro studies confirmed the mutations spliced out part of exon 4 and skipped exon 5, respectively, with both resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.
checks.explanation: The abstract says one child with SSMD carried two GPX4 variants, one inherited from the mother and one de novo. In vitro, both caused a frameshift and premature truncation. These are biallelic truncating mutations.

paragraphs.text: By whole-exome sequencing of a child with Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia and her unaffected parents, Smith et al. (2014) identified 2 rare variants in the GPX4 gene, which encodes glutathione peroxidase-4, in compound heterozygous state. In a second family, studied by Sanger sequencing, the affected child's DNA was unavailable, and the genotype was inferred from the carrier parents. Both mutations resulted in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4. Smith et al. (2014) concluded that the identification of truncating GPX4 mutations in 2 families supported the pathogenic role of mutated GPX4 in this disease.

checks.claim: Smith et al. (2014) performed whole-exome sequencing of a child with Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia and her unaffected parents.

checks.evidence_quote: The first (c.587+5G>A) was inherited from the mother, and the second (c.588-8_588-4del) was de novo (NM_001039848.1); both were predicted to impact splicing of GPX4.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports two rare variants, one maternal and one de novo, but never uses the term 'compound heterozygous' and does not establish phase.

checks.explanation: The abstract states that the child's DNA was unavailable and that the parents were studied by Sanger sequencing.

checks.claim: In the second family studied by Smith et al. (2014), the affected child's GPX4 genotype was inferred from the carrier parents.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not say 'inferred' outright, but this follows from the child's DNA being unavailable and both parents being carriers.

checks.claim: Both GPX4 mutations identified by Smith et al. (2014) resulted in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.
checks.evidence_quote: In vitro studies confirmed the mutations spliced out part of exon 4 and skipped exon 5, respectively, with both resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.
checks.explanation: The frameshift statement covers only the two splice variants in the first family. The second family's mutation is a stop mutation (p.Tyr127*), not a frameshift, and the draft's placement makes the claim ambiguous.

checks.claim: Smith et al. (2014) concluded that the identification of truncating GPX4 mutations in 2 families supported a pathogenic role of mutated GPX4 in Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Our identification of truncating mutations in GPX4 in two families affected with SSMD supports the pathogenic role of mutated GPX4 in this very rare disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.
